scenarios.answer: RFC 0043 — "Global Secrets/PII Redaction" — introduced the built-in secrets/PII redaction baseline. The motivation states that EKOS compiles raw file content from every connected system into an **append-only ledger**; because the ledger is append-only, once a secret is written it cannot be scrubbed out afterward. That is why redaction is a prevention problem: the baseline filter must be applied at every point raw file content enters the pipeline (observation artifacts, direct file reads), so no analyzer or future connector can forget to sanitize before content is committed to the ledger.

scenarios.answer: Devlog 100 records a real bug: a redaction false positive silently dropped a whole real Python file. The false positive occurred because the redaction logic in `crates/common/src/redaction.rs` treated a dotted chain of valid identifiers as a secret literal, even though real secret values are one contiguous alphanumeric/base64-ish run and never a dotted identifier chain; the fix added `skip_dotted_identifier_refs` to `SecretPattern`. Because the whole file was dropped, its compiled symbols were dropped along with it — the devlog notes that everything destroyed was EKOS-generated/regenerable or exactly recoverable from session context, and that the mechanism was a denial message not reflecting what actually happened. A later TODO also ties devlog_100 KC#2 to a redaction/analyzer logic change never re-scanning unchanged source.

scenarios.answer: The root cause was not a bug in the Python parser — it was a redaction false positive. Devlog 100 is titled "Redaction false positive silently dropped a whole real Python file," and the fix was in the redaction logic: `SecretPattern` in `crates/common/src/redaction.rs` gained `skip_dotted_identifier_refs: bool`, because real secret values are one contiguous alphanumeric/base64-ish run, never a dotted chain of valid identifiers. The missing symbols were a consequence of the whole Python file being dropped by that redaction false positive, not a parser failure.

It provides a Model Context Protocol server over **stdio** that exposes the read-only Runtime to AI agents, and it is referenced as the basis for later MCP transports (e.g., RFC 0143 MCP over Streamable HTTP) and for RFC 0018 Multi-hop Dependency & Impact Reasoning.
